issues.subcategory: Inconsistent test statistics between text and table
issues.description: In the Results section for Experiment 3, the text reports the go-past time effect as 'B = 41, t = 3.837' but Table 5 reports 'B = 43, t = 3.76'. Similarly, the regressions-out effect is reported in the text as 'B = 0.3, z = 3.12' but Table 5 reports 'B = 0.25, z = 2.65'. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the accuracy of the reported analyses.
issues.quote: There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001)

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent congruency effect magnitude
issues.description: The mean difference in go-past times between conditions reported in Table 5 is 507-458 = 49 ms, but the estimate B is reported as 43 in the table and 41 in the text. While B from a mixed model need not exactly equal the raw mean difference, the text also states the congruency effect is 49 ms (from the means), creating confusion about the actual effect size.

issues.subcategory: Incomplete reporting of token-based analysis in Experiment 2
issues.description: For Experiment 2's specificity analysis, the token-based interaction is reported as 'z = 0.60, p < 0.01'. A z-value of 0.60 would correspond to p ≈ 0.55, not p < 0.01. This is either a misreported z-value or a misreported p-value, representing a potentially serious statistical error.
issues.quote: As predicted, the interaction between specificity and condition was significant, such that the target spelling became used more often in the congruent condition than in the incongruent condition as its specificity increased (B = 1.9, z = 2.8, p < 0.01; for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01)

issues.subcategory: Missing power analysis
issues.description: No power analyses or sample size justifications are provided for any of the three experiments (N=46, N=29, N=47). Given that the key tests involve interactions between graded corpus-derived measures and experimental conditions, it is unclear whether these sample sizes provide adequate power, particularly for the moderation analyses.
issues.quote: Participants were 46 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway, University of London.

issues.subcategory: No random slopes in mixed models
issues.description: All mixed models include only random intercepts for subjects and suffixes but no random slopes for the fixed effects. Barr et al. (2013) have shown that omitting random slopes for within-subject/within-item factors can inflate Type I error rates substantially. The congruency manipulation is within-subjects and within-suffixes, so random slopes should be included or their omission justified.
issues.quote: This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject) + (1|suffix), data, family = "binomial").

issues.subcategory: No pre-registration or correction for multiple comparisons
issues.description: Experiment 3 tests six different eye-movement measures without correction for multiple comparisons. The authors acknowledge having no concrete predictions about which measures would be affected ('We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected'). This exploratory approach combined with no correction increases the risk of false positives. No pre-registration is mentioned.
issues.quote: We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation, so we chose to monitor a variety of typically studied measures

issues.subcategory: Missing data handling not fully described
issues.description: In Experiment 1, 11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or unrecognized button presses. This is a substantial proportion. No analysis is reported to determine whether missingness was related to condition (e.g., whether noun-diagnostic or adjective-diagnostic suffixes were more likely to time out), which could bias results.
issues.quote: 11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent suffix count after exclusion
issues.description: The text states that 64 suffixes occurring in fewer than 20 words were excluded, leaving 95 suffixes for analysis. However, 154 - 64 = 90, not 95. This arithmetic discrepancy suggests either the exclusion criterion or the remaining count is incorrect.
issues.quote: we excluded all suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 different words in the CELEX database, i.e. 64 suffixes... For the remaining 95 suffixes

issues.subcategory: Conflation of morphological and orthographic cues
issues.description: The experiments use nonwords with suffix spellings to test sensitivity to spelling-meaning regularities. However, the authors acknowledge that they 'did not include non-pseudoaffixed words because the goal of this experiment was not to adjudicate between types of cues used in lexical category judgement (e.g. orthographic vs morphological).' This means the experiments cannot distinguish whether participants are responding to morphological knowledge specifically or to broader orthographic distributional patterns, undermining the theoretical claims about morphological regularity.
issues.quote: We did not include non-pseudoaffixed words because the goal of this experiment was not to adjudicate between types of cues used in lexical category judgement (e.g. orthographic vs morphological).

issues.subcategory: Unmatched pre-target word count in Experiment 3
issues.description: The number of words before the target differed significantly between congruent and incongruent conditions (4.75 vs 5.23, p < 0.05). Although the authors conducted a follow-up analysis suggesting this did not affect results, this confound is problematic because more pre-target words could provide more syntactic context, potentially inflating the congruency effect.
issues.quote: Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05).

issues.subcategory: Comprehension accuracy reported as percentage not proportion
issues.description: Average comprehension accuracy is reported as '0.86%' which should presumably be 86% or 0.86 (proportion). As written, 0.86% would indicate near-zero accuracy. This appears to be a typographical error but creates ambiguity about task engagement.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%).

issues.subcategory: Sample limited to university students
issues.description: All three experiments use undergraduate students from a single university (Royal Holloway, University of London). The authors make broad claims about 'skilled readers' and 'the average reader' but the sample is restricted to young, highly educated individuals. This limits generalizability to the broader population of skilled readers.
issues.quote: We have shown that the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction to do so

issues.subcategory: Implicit learning claim without evidence
issues.description: The authors claim that the knowledge demonstrated in experiments was 'acquired through implicit statistical learning processes' and that participants were 'never taught these relationships explicitly.' However, no evidence is provided to rule out explicit instruction (e.g., grammar lessons about suffixes in school) or other learning mechanisms. The correlational nature of the data (corpus statistics predict behavior) does not establish the learning mechanism.
issues.quote: It is unlikely that our participants were ever taught these relationships explicitly; more likely is that this knowledge was acquired through implicit statistical learning processes

issues.subcategory: Marginal effects interpreted as supporting hypothesis
issues.description: In Experiment 3, the effect of diagnosticity on go-past times in the incongruent condition is described as 'a trend' at p = 0.13, and the effect on regressions-out in the incongruent condition is 'marginal' at p = 0.08. These non-significant effects are interpreted as supporting the hypothesis, which is problematic. The significant interaction should be interpreted cautiously when the simple effects in the predicted direction are not themselves significant.
issues.quote: whereas there was a trend towards an effect in the incongruent condition (B = 36.35, t = 1.58, p = 0.13)

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 lacks control for non-morphological cues
issues.description: Experiment 1 tests whether suffix spellings cue lexical category, but the nonwords contain only suffixed forms. Without a control condition using non-morphemic endings matched on orthographic properties, it is impossible to determine whether the effects are driven by morphological knowledge specifically or by general orthographic distributional knowledge.
issues.quote: We then asked adult skilled readers to make decisions as to whether the resulting nonwords appear more like adjectives or nouns.

issues.subcategory: Missing effect sizes
issues.description: No standardized effect sizes (e.g., Cohen's d, odds ratios with confidence intervals) are reported for any of the three experiments. Only unstandardized regression coefficients and test statistics are provided, making it difficult to evaluate the practical significance of the findings.
issues.quote: Results showed a main effect of suffix condition such that noun-diagnostic suffixes elicited more "noun" responses (B = -1.57, z = -4.224, p < 0.0001)

issues.subcategory: Sign transformation of diagnosticity variable
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the diagnosticity measure was multiplied by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes to create a single continuous predictor. This transformation assumes a linear relationship and imposes a specific functional form. The authors acknowledge this concern by running separate analyses, but the primary analysis relies on this transformation, which could introduce artifacts.
issues.quote: In order to investigate this statistically, we multiplied our diagnosticity measure by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes and substituted this measure in our model, in place of the condition variable.

issues.subcategory: Circularity in specificity computation
issues.description: Specificity is defined as the extent to which a suffix spelling is preferred for denoting a particular lexical category among all spellings of a sound sequence. However, the computation requires identifying which words contain 'suffix spellings' versus other spellings of the same sound, which presupposes morphological analysis. This creates a degree of circularity: the measure of how much a spelling signals meaning depends on prior identification of morphological structure.
issues.quote: we divided the number of words containing the suffix spelling (e.g. –LESS) by the total number of words of this lexical category with any spelling of the sound sequence

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 lacks counterbalancing of nonword-suffix pairings
issues.description: In Experiment 2, stems were joined with suffixes at random and each participant saw all 66 sentences. There is no counterbalancing of which stems appear with which suffixes or in which conditions across participants. This means that any idiosyncratic properties of specific nonwords could systematically influence results.
issues.quote: Sixty-six non-existing stems were selected from the same pool as in Experiment 1. Stems were joined with suffixes at random; one suffix was used with six different stems.

issues.subcategory: Incomplete model specification for Experiment 3
issues.description: For Experiment 3, the authors state 'All models included trial order as a main effect, and random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes' but do not provide the full model formula. Given the complexity of the analyses (including interactions with diagnosticity), the full model specifications should be reported for reproducibility.
issues.quote: All models included trial order as a main effect, and random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes. However, in the interest of space we report only those effects pertaining to our main variable of interest

issues.subcategory: Verb fillers excluded from analysis without justification for their inclusion
issues.description: In Experiment 3, 40 filler nonwords with verb suffixes were added but not analyzed because 'the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category.' If these suffixes are not diagnostic, their inclusion as fillers may have diluted participants' sensitivity to the manipulation or introduced noise, and this design choice should be better justified.
issues.quote: Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added so that sentence contexts would be more varied. These filler nonwords were not analysed, because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category (i.e. diagnosticity is less than 0.5).

issues.subcategory: Feedforward/feedback distinction not tested
issues.description: The authors hypothesize that diagnosticity should affect reading tasks (feedforward) while specificity should affect spelling tasks (feedback), but they do not test diagnosticity in the spelling task or specificity in the reading/classification tasks. This means the claimed dissociation between the two constructs is assumed rather than demonstrated.
issues.quote: we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the mapping of print to meaning... while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on spelling behaviour.

issues.subcategory: Entropy regression slope test methodology unclear
issues.description: The authors test whether the slope of the regression of Hspelling on Hphonology differs from 1 using an F-test with 1 degree of freedom. However, the methodology for this test is not clearly specified. Testing whether a slope differs from a specific value typically requires a t-test on (b-1)/SE(b), not an F-test. The reported values (slope = 0.9, SE = 0.04, which gives t = (0.9-1)/0.04 = -2.5, and F = 6.25) do not match the reported F(1) = 7.44.
issues.quote: We found that the regression line has a slope of 0.9 (SE = 0.04, t = 25.32, p < 0.0001), and that this slope is significantly different from 1 (F (1) = 7.44, p < 0.01).

issues.subcategory: CELEX database limitations
issues.description: The computational analysis relies entirely on the CELEX database, which is based on a specific corpus and may not reflect current English usage. CELEX was published in 1993 and its morphological annotations have known limitations. The authors do not discuss how database choice might affect their diagnosticity and specificity estimates.
issues.quote: We extracted all single-word entries from the CELEX database (Baayen, Piepenbrock & van Rijn, 1993)

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 timeout may bias results
issues.description: In Experiment 1, participants had a two-second timeout for their responses, and 11.7% of data were lost. The instructions stated that speed was not emphasized, yet a timeout was imposed. If certain suffix types were more difficult to categorize (leading to more timeouts), this could systematically bias the remaining data toward easier/more diagnostic suffixes.
issues.quote: Instructions did not emphasise speed, although participants needed to make their decisions within a two-second timeout period.

issues.subcategory: Lexical category as proxy for meaning
issues.description: The paper equates 'meaning' with lexical category throughout, but lexical category is only one aspect of meaning. The title claims to study 'meaningful regularities' and the abstract discusses 'meaningful information,' but the constructs measured (diagnosticity and specificity) only capture lexical category information, not semantic content. This overstates what the measures actually capture.
issues.quote: Diagnosticity captures the amount of meaningful information in a given spelling, whereas specificity estimates the degree of dispersion of this meaning across different spellings

issues.subcategory: Token diagnosticity results incompletely reported for Experiment 1
issues.description: The token-based analysis for Experiment 1 is mentioned only briefly, noting that adjective-specific suffixes did not show an effect (p > 0.8), but full statistics for the token-based analyses are not provided. Given that type and token measures diverge, complete reporting of both is important.
issues.quote: The results based on token measures were similar (main effect of diagnosticity, and an effect of diagnosticity on noun-diagnostic suffixes), but adjective-specific suffixes did not show an effect of diagnosticity (p > 0.8).

issues.subcategory: Sentence templates may introduce demand characteristics
issues.description: In Experiments 2 and 3, sentence contexts follow rigid templates (noun, adjective, verb). The formulaic nature of these templates (e.g., adjective contexts always use copular verbs like 'prove, stay, grow, smell, appear') may make the syntactic manipulation transparent to participants, potentially introducing demand characteristics, especially in the spelling task where participants see the sentence frame before hearing the nonword.
issues.quote: Nonwords in adjective contexts appeared after verbs prove, stay, grow, smell, appear, taste, sound, seem, look, turn, become, remain, that maximised the probability that they would be perceived as adjectives.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent description of Experiment 2 practice trials
issues.description: The text states 'Two additional practice trials we constructed' but this appears to be a grammatical error ('we' should be 'were'). More substantively, only 2 practice trials for 66 experimental items may be insufficient for participants to understand the task.
issues.quote: Two additional practice trials we constructed using nonwords and sentences that were not used in the main experiment.

issues.subcategory: Post-hoc selection of eye-movement measures
issues.description: The authors tested six eye-movement measures and found effects on only two (go-past time and regressions-out). The post-hoc interpretation that these measures specifically reflect 'disambiguation processes' and 'contextual integration' is consistent with the literature but was not predicted a priori. The selective interpretation of significant results among many tests raises concerns about analytic flexibility.
issues.quote: These results therefore indicate that the category information becomes important following initial lexical processing, when the reader has enough contextual information to understand the sentence and detect any incongruences.

issues.subcategory: Missing information about exclusion criteria for Experiment 3
issues.description: The eye-tracking data cleaning resulted in 4% of trials being discarded, but no breakdown is provided of how many were discarded per condition or per participant. If exclusions were uneven across conditions, this could bias results.
issues.quote: As a result of these checks, 4% of trials were discarded.
